desc:
Write the integers 1, 2, ..., n in a list sorted by their number of set bits (ones in binary) in ascending order; integers with the same number of set bits are ordered by value, smaller first. Return the k-th element of this list (1-indexed).

Example: for n = 10 the sorted list is 1, 2, 4, 8, 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 7 (one set bit, then two, then three). So k = 6 gives 5 and k = 10 gives 7.

The value of n is far too large to build and sort the list.
hints: Do not sort. Count how many integers in 1..n have exactly c set bits, for c = 1, 2, 3, ... and skip whole groups.
To count numbers in [0, x] with exactly c set bits, walk the bits of x from the top: at every set bit you may place a 0 there and choose the remaining bits freely, which gives a binomial coefficient.
First find the group c that contains the k-th element and the rank k' inside the group. Then binary search the smallest x with count(x, c) ≥ k'; the count is monotone in x.
editorial: Let count(x, c) be the number of integers in [0, x] with exactly c set bits. Scan the bits of x from the most significant one. Whenever x has a 1 at position i, every number that has the same higher bits as x but a 0 at position i is smaller than x, and its lower i bits are free, so it contributes C(i, c - ones) where ones is the number of set bits of x above position i. Finally x itself counts if it has exactly c set bits. This takes O(log x) per call.

Because c is at least 1, the integer 0 is never counted. Iterate c = 1, 2, ...: if k is at most count(n, c) the answer has c set bits; otherwise subtract count(n, c) from k and continue. At most 30 groups exist.

Inside the group, the elements are ordered by value, and count(x, c) is non-decreasing in x, so the answer is the smallest x with count(x, c) ≥ k (k now being the rank inside the group), found by binary search over [1, n] in about 30 steps. Total time O(log2 n), which is tiny.
